prompt:
You are a senior typographer and information designer. You lay out data tables for publication. You judge layouts by looking at the rendered result as a whole: what the table is for, how a reader scans and compares it, which columns belong together or play the same role, proportion and rhythm across columns, a clear hierarchy of headers and groups, whether rows read as units, whether words, numbers and identifiers stay intact, and how text and white space are distributed. Fewer lines or a shorter table is not automatically better, and neither is equal widths or symmetry; decide case by case and say why.

Table: 2024年10月员工工资条 (language zh-CN).
Grid: 8 columns × 8 rows. Row headers: yes (first logical column identifies each row).
Merged cells: "姓名" spans 1 col × 2 row; "应发" spans 3 col × 1 row; "扣款" spans 3 col × 1 row; "实发" spans 1 col × 2 row.
Per-column content facts (content px at 17px font, excluding padding):
  col 1: header "姓名" · longest unbreakable word 18px · one-line width 53px
  col 2: header "应发 › 基本工资" · longest unbreakable word 70px · one-line width 70px
  col 3: header "应发 › 绩效" · longest unbreakable word 65px · one-line width 65px
  col 4: header "应发 › 补贴" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 63px
  col 5: header "扣款 › 社保" · longest unbreakable word 56px · one-line width 56px
  col 6: header "扣款 › 公积金" · longest unbreakable word 63px · one-line width 63px
  col 7: header "扣款 › 个税" · longest unbreakable word 60px · one-line width 60px
  col 8: header "实发" · longest unbreakable word 71px · one-line width 71px
Each column also has 21px of padding+border, so a column given width w px shows w−21 px of text.
Available width: 601px (the dashed pink box = the reader's viewport). The column widths you choose must sum to at most 600px.
Fixed: content, font, 17px font size, padding, borders, colours, alignment. You control ONLY the column widths.

The image shows the table's content with every cell on one line, so you can read everything. Study it first.
1) Understand it: what is the table for, how will people read, scan and compare it, which columns play the same or similar role, which values must stay intact, which text may wrap naturally, and where existing row height could absorb wrapping.
2) Propose 3 genuinely different column-width designs for 601px (different strategies, not small variations).
An earlier design attempt for this table was rejected by independent reviewers. Their comments: another layout was rated bad: Nearly every monetary amount breaks across lines, including net pay, making rows and comparisons difficult to read. | another layout was rated poor: Names, two earnings columns, social insurance and net pay stay intact, but allowances, housing fund and tax amounts split across lines. | another layout was rated bad: Names stack character by character, and net pay extends beyond the viewport; both row identification and the final amounts suffer. | your previous preferred design was rated poor: Several important columns remain readable, but allowances, housing fund and tax amounts split, sometimes separating the decimal point from the rest of the number. | another layout was rated bad: Amounts split across nearly every earnings and deduction column, creating a repetitive field of fragments despite intact names and net pay. | another layout was rated poor: Names, all three earnings columns and net pay remain intact, but the three deduction columns break their amounts across lines.
another layout was rated poor: Names, base pay, performance pay, social insurance and net pay remain readable, but allowances, housing fund and tax amounts break across lines; the housing fund header also wraps. | another layout was rated bad: Nearly every monetary column breaks amounts across lines, including net pay, making payroll comparisons difficult. The base-pay header also wraps. | another layout was rated poor: Names, all earnings and net pay stay intact, giving the earnings group a clear rhythm. All three deduction columns split their amounts, and the housing fund header wraps. | another layout was rated bad: Names are stacked character by character, making row identification difficult, and net pay extends beyond the viewport. Most other amounts remain intact. | your previous preferred design was rated poor: Names, base pay, performance pay, social insurance and net pay remain intact, but allowances, housing fund and tax amounts split across lines; the housing fund header also wraps. | another layout was rated bad: Names and net pay remain intact, but amounts across all six earnings and deduction columns wrap, weakening row reading and comparison. Two headers also wrap.
